## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- **Explain** Kirchhoff's three laws and predict which spectrum a source produces
- **Interpret** the Bohr model to explain why spectral lines have specific wavelengths
- **Classify** stars by spectral type (OBAFGKM) as a **temperature** sequence
- **Apply** the Doppler shift to measure stellar radial velocities
- **Connect** spectral absorption to the greenhouse effect
:::

::: {.notes}
Read aloud. ~1 min. Students should note these — they map to what's testable.
:::

::: {.r-fit-text}
All stars are ~73% hydrogen and ~25% helium.

So why do their spectra look so different?
:::

::: {.notes}
0–1 min. Let this sit for 5 seconds. Don't answer yet.

This is the throughline question for the whole lecture. The answer (temperature controls which energy levels are populated) won't land until Part 3, but planting it now gives students a reason to pay attention.

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Kirchhoff's Laws
:::

*Three spectra, three physical setups*

---

## Three Types of Spectra {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
{{< fig three-types-of-spectra >}}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.text-sm}
1. **Continuous** — hot, dense source → all wavelengths (Planck curve)
2. **Emission** — hot, low-density gas → bright lines on dark background
3. **Absorption** — cooler gas in front of hot continuum → dark lines
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
The **same gas** produces emission OR absorption depending on what's behind it.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
2–3 min. Point to each type in the figure. Reveal the list, then the fragment. Emphasize that the physical setup — not the gas itself — determines which type you see.
:::

---

## Quick Label (30 seconds) {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

For each spectrum type, write down: **(1)** the type and **(2)** the physical setup in six words or fewer.

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
**Example format:**

- *Continuous — hot, dense source emits all wavelengths.*
- *Emission — hot, thin gas emits bright lines.*
- *Absorption — cool gas blocks specific colors.*
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
~3 min. 30-second micro-task. Let students write, then reveal the example answers. This cements the three types before formalizing them as Kirchhoff's laws.
:::

---

## Kirchhoff's Three Laws

::: {.incremental}
1. **Hot, dense source** → continuous spectrum (all wavelengths)
2. **Hot, low-density gas** → emission lines (bright lines, dark background)
3. **Cooler gas in front of hot continuum** → absorption lines (dark lines in rainbow)
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
The **same gas** absorbs at the **same wavelengths** it would emit.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
3–4 min. Reveal one at a time. Stress law 3: the absorption wavelengths match the emission wavelengths — Kirchhoff noticed this empirically.
:::

---

## The Reverse Problem

::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
In practice, you work Kirchhoff's laws **backwards:**

Given a spectrum → infer the physical configuration.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.text-sm}
- Dark lines in a rainbow? → cooler gas in front of a hotter continuum
- Bright lines on dark background? → hot, tenuous gas, no continuum behind it
- Smooth rainbow, no lines? → hot, dense source
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
**This is the skill you'll use for the rest of the course.**
:::

::: {.notes}
~4 min. Quick reframe. The "reverse problem" is the working-astronomer mindset: you start with data, not theory. You see a spectrum and deduce the physics. Stress that this is the same logic for every spectrum they'll encounter.
:::

---

## Why Stars Show Absorption Spectra {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
{{< fig week04-photosphere-line-formation-cococubed >}}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.text-sm}
**Two-layer model:**

1. **Photosphere** ($\tau \approx 1$) — hot, dense → continuous spectrum (Law 1)
2. **Atmosphere** (cooler, above) → absorbs at specific wavelengths (Law 3)
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .mt-1}
We see: a **continuous rainbow with dark lines** carved into it.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
Temperature decreases outward — that's why absorption, not emission.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
4–5 min. Walk through the two-layer model. The photosphere is where optical depth $\tau \approx 1$ — the depth where the star becomes opaque. The cooler atmosphere above it absorbs at specific wavelengths.
:::

---

## Two Myths to Kill Now {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

Plant these flags before we go further:

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
**Myth 1: "Spectral type tells me what a star is made of."**

It doesn't — not directly. Spectral type primarily reflects *temperature*. Stars of wildly different types have nearly identical compositions. (Part 3 will prove this.)
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-1}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
**Myth 2: "A redshifted star looks red."**

It doesn't. "Redshift" means lines shift to *longer wavelengths* — a fractional change of ~0.01%. A blue O star receding from you is still blue. (Part 4 makes this quantitative.)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
~5 min. Deliver these as firm corrections. Students who build the wrong mental model here will struggle for weeks. These same myths appear in the reading's "Two Myths to Kill Now" box — reinforce here so students hear it twice.
:::

---

## Observable → Model → Inference

::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
- **Observable:** Dark lines at specific wavelengths in a stellar spectrum
- **Model:** Kirchhoff's third law — cooler atmosphere absorbs from hotter photosphere
- **Inference:** The star has a hot interior surrounded by a cooler atmosphere
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
The dark lines are the key to **everything** that follows.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
🔍 **Spectrum Detective — Clue 0:** The *shape* of the spectrum (continuous vs. lines, absorption vs. emission) tells you the *physical setup* of the source.
:::

::: {.notes}
6–7 min. This is the O→M→I frame for the whole lecture. Every dark line encodes physics. The "Spectrum Detective" motif runs through the reading — plant the first clue here.
:::

---

## Prediction: Which Spectrum? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

You look at a **glowing neon sign** through a spectrograph.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
**Commit to one answer:**

(a) Continuous spectrum — smooth rainbow

(b) Emission spectrum — bright lines on dark background

(c) Absorption spectrum — dark lines in a rainbow
:::

::: {.notes}
7–8 min. Give 30 seconds. Cold-call 2 students.

Answer: **(b) Emission.** Neon is a hot, low-density gas (Kirchhoff's law 2). No hot dense source behind it → no continuum to absorb from.
:::

---

## Think–Pair–Share: Design a Kirchhoff Test {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Scenario:** You have a hydrogen gas tube and a bright white lamp.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
1. How would you set up an experiment to produce a hydrogen **emission** spectrum?
2. How would you rearrange to produce a hydrogen **absorption** spectrum?
3. Which Kirchhoff law governs each setup?
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
*30 seconds alone → 1 minute with a neighbor → share out*
:::

::: {.notes}
8–10 min. This is a TPS — give time for genuine discussion.

(1) Heat the gas tube alone; observe its light → emission (law 2).
(2) Place the gas tube between the white lamp and spectrograph → absorption (law 3).
(3) The gas tube must be cooler than the lamp's continuum for absorption lines to appear.

Cold-call 1–2 pairs for their design.
:::

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Spectral Lines as Atomic Fingerprints
:::

*The Bohr model and discrete energy levels*

---

## The Bohr Model: Discrete Energy Levels {background-color="black"}

{{< fig hydrogen-absorption >}}

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Electrons occupy **specific energy rungs** — they cannot hover between them.
:::

::: {.notes}
10–12 min. Point to the energy levels in the diagram.

Key idea: electrons can only be at certain energies. To absorb a photon, the photon's energy must **exactly match** a gap between levels. This is why absorption happens at specific wavelengths.
:::

---

## The Reverse: Emission {background-color="black"}

{{< fig hydrogen-emission >}}

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Same energy gaps → same wavelengths — whether absorbing or emitting.
:::

::: {.notes}
~12 min. Quick. Same gaps, same wavelengths. This is why Kirchhoff's observation works: the gas absorbs at the same wavelengths it emits.
:::

---

## Hydrogen Energy Levels

$$E_n = -\frac{13.6\ \text{eV}}{n^2}$$

::: {.fragment}
- $n = 1$ (ground state): $E_1 = -13.6$ eV — most tightly bound
- $n = 2$: $E_2 = -3.4$ eV
- $n \to \infty$: $E = 0$ — electron is free (ionized)
:::

::: {.fragment .highlight-red}
**Negative sign** = the electron is *bound*. You must add energy to free it.
:::

::: {.notes}
12–13 min. Walk through the levels slowly. The minus sign confuses students — address it directly. "More negative = more tightly bound."
:::

---

## Spectral Lines Come from Transitions

When an electron jumps between levels:

$$\Delta E = |E_{\text{upper}} - E_{\text{lower}}|$$

. . .

The photon's wavelength is set by the energy gap:

$$\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Different elements → different energy levels → different spectral lines.**
:::

::: {.notes}
13–14 min. This is the core mechanism. Each element has a unique set of energy levels, so each element produces a unique barcode of spectral lines.
:::

---

## The Balmer Series: Hydrogen's Visible Fingerprint

Transitions to/from $n = 2$:

::: {.table-scroll .text-sm}
| Transition | Name | Wavelength | Color |
|---|---|---|---|
| $n = 3 \to 2$ | H$\alpha$ | 656 nm | Deep red |
| $n = 4 \to 2$ | H$\beta$ | 486 nm | Blue-green |
| $n = 5 \to 2$ | H$\gamma$ | 434 nm | Violet |
| $n = 6 \to 2$ | H$\delta$ | 410 nm | Near-UV |
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Energy gaps of ~1.9–3.0 eV → visible wavelengths.
:::

::: {.notes}
14–15 min. These are the most important spectral lines in stellar astronomy. H$\alpha$ is the red glow in nebula photos.
:::

---

## Worked Example: Calculating H$\alpha$

**Problem:** Predict the wavelength of $n = 3 \to 2$ in hydrogen.

. . .

**Step 1 — Energy levels:**

$$E_3 = \frac{-13.6\ \text{eV}}{9} = -1.51\ \text{eV} \qquad E_2 = \frac{-13.6\ \text{eV}}{4} = -3.40\ \text{eV}$$

. . .

**Step 2 — Energy gap:**

$$\Delta E = |-1.51\ \text{eV} - (-3.40\ \text{eV})| = 1.89\ \text{eV}$$

. . .

**Step 3 — CGS conversion:** ($1\ \text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{erg}$)

$$\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E} = \frac{1.986 \times 10^{-16}\ \text{erg·cm}}{3.03 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{erg}} = 6.56 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{cm} = 656\ \text{nm}\ \checkmark$$

::: {.notes}
15–16 min. Walk through step by step. Every intermediate value carries its unit — eV on every numerator, eV on every subtraction. This is the full CGS grind; the shortcut comes next.
:::

---

## The $hc$ Shortcut — Your Default Tool

For any transition with energy gap $\Delta E$ (in eV):

$$\lambda\ (\text{nm}) \approx \frac{1240\ \text{eV·nm}}{\Delta E\ (\text{eV})}$$

::: {.fragment}
**For H$\alpha$:**

$$\lambda \approx \frac{1240\ \text{eV·nm}}{1.89\ \text{eV}} \approx 656\ \text{nm}\ \checkmark$$
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Same answer, one line. **Use $hc \approx 1240\ \text{eV·nm}$ freely** unless a problem asks for CGS.
:::

::: {.notes}
~17 min. This shortcut is designated as the default tool for ASTR 201. Students should memorize $hc \approx 1240$ eV·nm. The full CGS derivation is for "show your work" problems; this is for quick estimates and sanity checks.
:::

---

## Every Element Has a Unique Barcode {background-color="black"}

{{< fig absorption-emission-elements >}}

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Match observed lines to laboratory wavelengths → **identify the element.**
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
🔍 **Spectrum Detective — Clue 1:** The *positions* of absorption lines tell you which **elements** are present — each element's fingerprint is unique.
:::

::: {.notes}
17–18 min. This is the payoff: we identify elements in stars by matching their spectral barcode to lab data. No need to visit the star.
:::

---

## Real Data: Altair's Spectrum {background-color="black"}

{{< fig altair-spectrum-annotated >}}

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
**Two tools in one observation:** the curve gives temperature (Wien), the lines give composition.
:::

::: {.notes}
18–19 min. Point to the smooth blackbody-like envelope → gives the temperature. Point to the dark dips → those are absorption lines, primarily hydrogen Balmer series. This is what a real stellar spectrum looks like when you spread starlight through a spectrograph. Altair is an A7V star — strong Balmer lines, as expected.
:::

---

## Think–Pair–Share: Mystery Element {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

A star's spectrum shows absorption lines at **393.4 nm** and **396.8 nm** — but hydrogen has no transitions at these wavelengths.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
1. Are these lines from hydrogen? How do you know?
2. These are the **Ca II H & K lines** (ionized calcium). What does "ionized" tell you about the temperature?
3. In which spectral type(s) would you expect these lines to be strongest?
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
*30 seconds alone → 1 minute with a neighbor → share out*
:::

::: {.notes}
19–21 min. This is a genuine mystery-solving exercise.

(1) No — hydrogen Balmer lines are at 410, 434, 486, 656 nm. These don't match.
(2) Ca II means calcium has lost one electron. This requires moderate temperature — enough to ionize Ca but not strip it further.
(3) Ca II H & K lines are strongest in **G and K stars** (like the Sun). Too hot (O, B) and calcium is multiply ionized; too cool (M) and it's mostly neutral.

Cold-call 1 pair. These are the strongest lines in the solar spectrum — important to recognize.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Spectral Lines {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
An absorption line appears at 486.1 nm in a star's spectrum. Which element and transition is this?

- [ ] Helium, ground-state transition
- [x] Hydrogen, $n = 4 \to 2$ (H$\beta$)
- [ ] Sodium, D-line transition
- [ ] Iron, ionized state
:::

::: {.notes}
~22 min. Give 20–30 seconds.

Correct: 486.1 nm is H$\beta$, the second Balmer line. Students should be learning to recognize these numbers.
:::

## The Harvard Computers {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
{{< fig harvard-computers >}}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.text-sm}
500,000 glass plates. Millions of spectra. No automation.

::: {.fragment}
- **Williamina Fleming** — first classification system, 310 variable stars, Horsehead Nebula
- **Annie Jump Cannon** — 350,000 spectra classified, OBAFGKM sequence
- **Antonia Maury** — noticed line *widths* vary → luminosity class
:::
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
Hired as cheap labor (25–50¢/hr, less than secretaries), denied telescope access — and they transformed astronomy.
:::

::: {.notes}
22–23 min. Frame this as the "industrial data problem": two technologies (spectroscopy + photography) created a data bottleneck. Pickering hired women because they were educated, available, and cheap. The classification work was NOT clerical — it required recognizing subtle patterns in noisy photographic data, statistical pattern recognition before formal statistics.
:::

---

## Data First, Theory Later

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
**The Harvard classifications demanded explanation:**

- **1925:** Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin proved stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen & helium — arguably the most important PhD in astronomy. Her advisor Russell called it "clearly impossible" before later admitting she was right.
- **1920s:** Eddington's stellar models explained OBAFGKM as a temperature sequence.
- **1938:** Bethe's nuclear fusion theory completed the picture.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
The pattern was observed first. The physics was built to explain it.

**This is Observable → Model → Inference in its purest historical form.**
:::

::: {.notes}
~24 min. This slide connects the Harvard Computers to the course's O→M→I framework. The spectral sequence was empirical — the Boltzmann distribution and Saha equation came later to explain *why* it exists. This is how science usually works, even when textbooks present it the other way around.
:::

---

## The Spectral Sequence {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
{{< fig obafgkm-spectra >}}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.text-sm}
From top to bottom: **O → B → A → F → G → K → M**

- Hot (O): ionized helium lines
- Middle (A): strongest hydrogen Balmer lines
- Cool (M): molecular bands (TiO)
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
Spectral features change dramatically — but **composition is nearly the same** across all types.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .mt-1}
**Oh Be A Fine Guy/Girl, Kiss Me.**
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
24–25 min. Walk through the sequence from O (hot, blue) to M (cool, red). Point to how the spectral features change dramatically even though composition is ~the same.
:::

---

## OBAFGKM at a Glance

::: {.table-scroll .text-xs}
| Type | Color | Temperature | Main-Seq. Prevalence | Dominant Features |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| O | Blue-violet | $\gtrsim 30{,}000$ K | 0.00003% | Ionized helium |
| B | Blue-white | 10,000–30,000 K | 0.13% | Neutral helium, strong H |
| **A** | White | 7,500–10,000 K | 0.6% | **Strongest H Balmer** |
| F | Yellow-white | 6,000–7,500 K | 3% | Moderate H, weak metals |
| **G** | Yellow | 5,200–6,000 K | 7.6% | Weak H, **strong metals** |
| K | Orange | 3,700–5,200 K | 12.1% | Very weak H, molecular bands |
| **M** | Red-orange | $\lesssim 3{,}700$ K | 76.5% | **TiO molecular bands** |
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
M dwarfs are **76.5%** of all stars — too faint to see by eye.
:::

::: {.notes}
25–26 min. Don't read the whole table. Highlight three things:

1. A stars have strongest H lines
2. G stars (like the Sun) show strong metal lines
3. M dwarfs dominate the galaxy by number
:::

---

## Four Knobs, One Spectrum

::: {.table-scroll .text-xs}
| What You Measure | What It Tells You |
|---|---|
| **Line positions** (which wavelengths are dark) | **Composition** — which elements are present |
| **Line strength pattern** (which species dominate) | **Temperature** → spectral type (OBAFGKM) |
| **Line widths** (narrow vs. broad) | **Surface gravity / rotation** → luminosity class |
| **Metal line forest** (amplitude relative to H) | **Metallicity** (heavy-element abundance) |
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Temperature is the dominant knob — it controls line strengths so powerfully that it can mask composition differences entirely.
:::

::: {.notes}
~26 min. This table is from the reading. Temperature is the first-order effect; metallicity and gravity are second-order. The table gives students a mental checklist for reading any spectrum.
:::

---

## Why Temperature Controls Line Strength

::: {.incremental}
- For H absorption: electron must already be in $n = 2$
- Fraction in $n = 2$ depends on temperature: $\propto e^{-\chi_2/k_BT}$
- [**Too cool (M stars):**]{.rn rn-type="underline" rn-color="#ff6b6b"} almost no atoms in $n = 2$ → weak H lines
- [**Just right (A stars):**]{.rn rn-type="box" rn-color="#4ecdc4"} maximum population in $n = 2$ → strongest H lines
- [**Too hot (O stars):**]{.rn rn-type="underline" rn-color="#ff6b6b"} hydrogen is **ionized** → no neutral H → weak H lines
:::

::: {.notes}
26–28 min. This is the hardest conceptual point. Walk slowly.

The Boltzmann factor $e^{-\chi/kT}$ with $\chi_2 = 10.2$ eV means you need T ~ 10,000 K to populate $n = 2$ significantly. But go too hot and hydrogen ionizes entirely. The "sweet spot" is A-star temperatures.
:::

---

## Predict First: Which Type Wins? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

All stars are ~73% hydrogen. Hydrogen Balmer absorption requires electrons already in $n = 2$, which is **10.2 eV** above the ground state.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm .mt-2}
At which spectral type — **O, A, G, or M** — would you expect the **strongest** Balmer lines, and why?

*Commit to an answer before I show you.*
:::

::: {.notes}
~28 min. Give 30 seconds. Do NOT reveal the answer — let the next slide do that. This is a "Predict First" moment from the reading. Students who commit to a prediction learn more from the explanation.
:::

---

## The Goldilocks Problem: A Balmer Line Peak

::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
**Two competing effects at work:**

1. **Excitation** ($\propto e^{-\chi_2/k_BT}$): hotter → more atoms in $n = 2$
2. **Ionization**: hotter → more atoms lose electrons entirely
:::

. . .

::: {.table-scroll .text-sm}
| Temperature | Excitation | Ionization | Balmer strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3,000 K (M) | Very low | Negligible | **Weak** — no $n=2$ |
| 10,000 K (A) | High | Moderate | **Peak** — sweet spot |
| 35,000 K (O) | Very high | Nearly complete | **Weak** — no neutral H |
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Balmer strength rises, peaks at A stars, then falls — a **competition**, not monotonic growth.
:::

::: {.notes}
28–30 min. Draw this out as a sketch if chalkboard is handy: x-axis = temperature, y-axis = Balmer line strength. The curve rises from M, peaks at A, and falls again at O. This non-monotonic behavior is what makes the spectral sequence surprising and what Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin had to explain.
:::

---

## Prediction: Why Weak H Lines? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

An M star ($T \approx 3{,}000$ K) has **weak** hydrogen Balmer lines.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
**Which explanation is correct?**

(a) M stars have very little hydrogen

(b) M stars are too cool — almost no H atoms in the $n = 2$ state

(c) M stars are so hot that hydrogen is ionized

(d) M stars are too far away to show lines
:::

::: {.notes}
~31 min. Give 30 seconds. Cold-call.

Answer: **(b).** All stars have ~73% hydrogen. But at 3,000 K, the Boltzmann factor puts almost no atoms in $n = 2$, so Balmer absorption is extremely weak.

This directly answers the hook question from the beginning!
:::

---

## The Spectral Sequence Is Temperature {background-color="black"}

::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
- **Do O stars have more helium?** No — same composition. Temperature ionizes H and excites He.
- **Do A stars have more hydrogen?** No — same abundance. Temperature puts H into $n = 2$.
- **Do M stars lack hydrogen?** No. Temperature keeps H atoms in $n = 1$ (ground state).
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-lg .font-semibold .mt-2}
Same atoms. Different temperatures. Different spectra.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
🔍 **Spectrum Detective — Clue 2:** The *pattern* of line strengths tells you **temperature** (spectral type). Strong Balmer? ~10,000 K. TiO bands? Below ~3,700 K.
:::

::: {.notes}
31–32 min. This is the punchline that answers the opening question. Land it clearly. Clue 2 completes the temperature inference.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Spectral Type {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
Two stars have identical composition. Star X is spectral type A; Star Y is spectral type M. What's different?

- [ ] Star X has more hydrogen
- [ ] Star Y has more metals
- [x] Star X is hotter, so more H atoms occupy the $n = 2$ level
- [ ] Star Y is closer, so lines appear weaker
:::

::: {.notes}
~33 min. Give 20 seconds.

Correct: temperature controls level populations, not composition.
:::

---

## Metallicity: A Secondary Effect

**Metallicity** ($Z$) = mass fraction of elements heavier than helium.

::: {.incremental}
- Sun: $Z_\odot \approx 0.014$ — about 1.4% "metals"
- High-$Z$ stars: more and stronger metal absorption lines
- Low-$Z$ stars: "cleaner" spectra with fewer metal lines
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
**But metallicity is second-order for classification.** Two stars at the same temperature with different $Z$ have the **same spectral type** — the metal line strengths differ, but which species dominates is set by temperature.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
33–34 min. Quick slide. Metallicity matters for detailed chemical abundance work, but it doesn't change the spectral type itself. The OBAFGKM system is primarily a temperature sequence.

Fun fact: in astronomy, everything heavier than helium is a "metal." Carbon, oxygen, iron — all "metals."
:::

---

## Beyond Temperature: What Line Widths Reveal {background-color="black"}

{{< fig mk-star-sizes >}}

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
- **Giants/supergiants:** low-density atmospheres → [narrow]{.rn rn-type="underline" rn-color="#4ecdc4"} spectral lines
- **Dwarfs (main-sequence):** compact, dense atmospheres → [broad]{.rn rn-type="underline" rn-color="#ff6b6b"} spectral lines
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
**G2V** (Sun) and **G2Ib** (supergiant): same temperature, wildly different size and luminosity.
:::

::: {.notes}
34–35 min. Introduce the Morgan–Keenan luminosity class briefly. The Roman numeral (V = dwarf, III = giant, I = supergiant) encodes surface gravity, which spectroscopists read from line widths. An M supergiant (Betelgeuse, M2Ia) can be more luminous than a hot O dwarf — temperature ≠ luminosity.

We'll use this extensively when we build the full H–R diagram in Lectures 5–6.
:::

---

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
The Doppler Shift
:::

*Reading stellar motion from light*

---

## Doppler: Wavelength Shifts from Motion {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
{{< fig doppler-shift-exoplanet >}}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.text-sm}
Motion along the line of sight shifts **all** spectral lines:

- **Receding** → lines shift to longer wavelengths (**redshift**)
- **Approaching** → lines shift to shorter wavelengths (**blueshift**)
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
Typical stellar velocities: 10–100 km/s → shifts of only ~0.01–0.03%, but **measurable**.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
36–37 min. Connect to sound analogy (ambulance siren) but keep it brief — go straight to the formula on the next slide.
:::

---

## The Doppler Formula

$$\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0} = \frac{v_r}{c}$$

::: {.fragment}
- $\Delta\lambda = \lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_0$ — the shift
- $v_r$ — radial velocity (+ = receding, − = approaching)
- $c = 3.0 \times 10^5$ km/s — speed of light
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
**Redshift** ($\Delta\lambda > 0$): source receding | **Blueshift** ($\Delta\lambda < 0$): source approaching
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
**Diagnostic:** A real Doppler shift moves *all* lines by the same fraction $\Delta\lambda/\lambda_0$. If only one line shifts — it's a misidentification, not motion.
:::

::: {.notes}
37–38 min. Both sides are dimensionless ratios. Stress: typical stellar velocities are 10–100 km/s, so shifts are tiny (~0.01–0.03%) but measurable. The diagnostic about all lines shifting by the same fraction is a crucial practical check — students will need this when analyzing real spectra.
:::

---

## Worked Example: Radial Velocity from H$\alpha$

**Problem:** H$\alpha$ observed at 656.5 nm (rest: 656.3 nm). Approaching or receding?

. . .

**Step 1 — Direction:** $\lambda_{\text{obs}} > \lambda_0$ → **redshifted** → **receding**

. . .

**Step 2 — Shift:** $\Delta\lambda = 656.5 - 656.3 = 0.2$ nm

. . .

**Step 3 — Velocity:**

$$v_r = c \times \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda_0} = (3.0 \times 10^5\ \text{km/s}) \times \frac{0.2}{656.3} \approx 91\ \text{km/s}$$

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
A 0.03% shift → ~91 km/s. Tiny shift, huge velocity.
:::

::: {.notes}
38–39 min. Walk each step. Unit check: (km/s) × (nm/nm) = km/s ✓. Emphasize how a 0.2 nm shift is barely perceptible but translates to ~91 km/s because $c$ is enormous.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Doppler Direction {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
H$\beta$ (rest: 486.1 nm) is observed at 485.9 nm. The star is…

- [x] Approaching (blueshifted — observed wavelength is shorter)
- [ ] Receding (redshifted)
- [ ] Stationary (no shift)
- [ ] Rotating (broadened)
:::

::: {.notes}
~39 min. Give 20 seconds.

$\lambda_{\text{obs}} < \lambda_0$ → blueshift → approaching. The velocity would be $v_r = c \times (-0.2/486.1) \approx -123$ km/s.
:::

---

## Think–Pair–Share: Exoplanet Wobble {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

A star's H$\alpha$ line oscillates between 656.25 nm and 656.35 nm over a 4-day cycle. The rest wavelength is 656.3 nm.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
1. Is the star moving? How do you know?
2. What is the velocity amplitude ($v_r$) of the wobble?
3. What could cause a **periodic** Doppler oscillation?
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
*30 seconds alone → 1 minute with a neighbor → share out*
:::

::: {.notes}
39–42 min. This previews Lecture 4 (binary stars) and exoplanet detection.

(1) Yes — the line shifts back and forth around the rest wavelength.
(2) $\Delta\lambda = \pm 0.05$ nm → $v_r = c \times 0.05/656.3 \approx \pm 23$ km/s.
(3) An **orbiting companion** (planet or another star) tugs the star back and forth. The 4-day period is the orbital period. This is radial velocity exoplanet detection — the same technique that found the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star (51 Peg b, 1995).

Cold-call 1–2 pairs. Emphasize: Doppler isn't just a velocity tool — it finds invisible companions.
:::

---

## Doppler Unlocks Masses {background-color="black"}

::: {.bg-muted .p-2}
If a star is in a **binary system**, its radial velocity oscillates as it orbits.

Measure the oscillation period and amplitude → infer the companion's **mass**.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-lg .font-semibold .mt-2}
**Lecture 4:** Binary orbits + Doppler → stellar masses.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
🔍 **Spectrum Detective — Clue 3:** The *shifts* of line positions — every line offset by the same fraction — tell you the star's **radial velocity**.
:::

::: {.notes}
42–43 min. Forward pointer. Doppler isn't just a velocity tool — it's the most direct route to stellar masses, which determine everything about stellar evolution.
:::

---

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Putting It Together
:::

*Three clues from one spectrum*

---

## One Spectrum, Four Inferences {background-color="black"}

::: {.table-scroll .text-xs}
| Observable | What we measure | What we infer |
|---|---|---|
| **Line positions** (which wavelengths are dark) | Wavelengths matched to lab data | **Composition** |
| **Line strength pattern** (which species dominate) | Relative strengths | **Temperature** → spectral type |
| **Line shifts** (offset from lab wavelengths) | Doppler shift $\Delta\lambda/\lambda_0$ | **Radial velocity** |
| **Line widths** (narrow vs. broad) | Pressure/rotational broadening | **Surface gravity** → luminosity class |
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Composition, temperature, motion, and size — from a single observation.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
🔍 **Spectrum Detective — Case Closed.** All clues collected: composition (Clue 1), temperature (Clue 2), velocity (Clue 3). Three independent measurements, one observation.
:::

::: {.notes}
43–44 min. This is the synthesis moment. Four pieces of information from one spectrum. The Spectrum Detective motif from the reading wraps up here.
:::

---

## Multi-Clue Diagnosis

**Observed:** $T \approx 9{,}500$ K, strong Balmer lines, weak metals, H$\alpha$ at 656.1 nm

. . .

**(a) Spectral type:** ~9,500 K + strong Balmer → **type A**

. . .

**(b) Velocity:** $\Delta\lambda = 656.1 - 656.3 = -0.2$ nm → blueshifted → approaching

$$v_r = (3.0 \times 10^5) \times \frac{-0.2}{656.3} \approx -91\ \text{km/s}$$

. . .

**(c) What else do we need?** Distance → luminosity → radius. Time-series Doppler → mass.

::: {.notes}
44–45 min. This worked example ties everything together. Reveal progressively. Each step uses a different tool from the lecture.
:::

Enter: **Plate 285, MJD 51930, Fiber 164** (a classic A star).

## {.center}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Spectroscopy Meets Climate
:::

*Same physics, different scale*

---

## Planetary Energy Balance

At equilibrium: power absorbed from star = power radiated by planet.

::: {.fragment}
$$T_{\text{eq}} = 279\ \text{K} \times (1-A)^{1/4} \times \left(\frac{d}{1\ \text{AU}}\right)^{-1/2}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
For Earth ($A = 0.3$, $d = 1$ AU):

$$T_{\text{eq}} = 279 \times (0.70)^{1/4} \times 1 = 279 \times 0.915 = 255\ \text{K} = -18°\text{C}$$
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
**Earth's actual average: 288 K = +15°C.** Something warms us by 33 K.
:::

::: {.notes}
47–48 min. The ratio method makes this quick. Emphasize: 255 K is well below freezing — without the greenhouse effect, Earth would be an ice ball.
:::

---

## Predict First: What Warms Earth? {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

Earth's equilibrium temperature is 255 K — well below freezing.

The observed average is 288 K — above freezing.

::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm .mt-2}
What must the atmosphere be doing to account for that **33 K** difference?

Think about Kirchhoff's third law applied to a *planet* instead of a star.
:::

::: {.notes}
~47 min. Give 20–30 seconds. The atmosphere is the "cool gas" absorbing from the "hot continuum" (Earth's surface thermal emission). Students should connect: the same law that explains stellar absorption lines also explains planetary warming. Don't answer yet — the next slide does.
:::

---

## The Greenhouse Effect: Kirchhoff's Law 3 for Planets {background-color="black"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
{{< fig earth-energy-balance-blackbodies >}}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.text-sm}
**Two Planck curves:**

1. **Sun → Earth** peaks at ~0.5 μm (visible) — passes through atmosphere
2. **Earth → space** peaks at ~10 μm (IR) — **blocked by greenhouse gases**
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .mt-1}
CO$_2$, H$_2$O, CH$_4$ absorb outgoing IR and re-emit some **back down** → surface warms.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-sm .text-muted .mt-1}
This IS Kirchhoff's Law 3: atmosphere = "cool gas" absorbing from the "hot continuum" (Earth's surface).
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
48–49 min. Point to the two Planck curves in the figure. The atmosphere is transparent at visible wavelengths but opaque at thermal IR — that asymmetry is the entire greenhouse mechanism.
:::

---

## A Tale of Three Planets {background-color="black"}

{{< fig greenhouse-comparison >}}

::: {.table-scroll .text-xs}
| Planet | $T_{\text{eq}}$ (K) | Actual $T$ (K) | Greenhouse warming |
|---|---|---|---|
| Venus | 227 | **735** | +508 K |
| Earth | 255 | **288** | +33 K |
| Mars | 210 | **210** | ~0 K |
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Same star, similar compositions. **Atmosphere thickness** makes all the difference.
:::

::: {.notes}
49–50 min. Venus: runaway greenhouse, CO₂ at 92 bar, hot enough to melt lead. Mars: CO₂ atmosphere but only 0.6% of Earth's pressure → negligible greenhouse. Earth: just right — for now.

Note the paradox: Venus has a LOWER equilibrium temperature than Earth (high albedo reflects most sunlight), yet it's 460°C at the surface. That's how powerful the greenhouse effect is.
:::

---

## CO$_2$'s 15 $\mu\text{m}$ Band {background-color="black"}

{{< fig earth-reflectance-spectra >}}

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
CO$_2$ absorbs at 15 $\mu\text{m}$ — right where Earth's thermal radiation peaks.
:::

::: {.notes}
50–51 min. Point to the 15 μm absorption dip. This is the same quantum mechanics as hydrogen Balmer lines — molecular energy levels producing absorption at specific wavelengths. Adding more CO₂ deepens and broadens this band, trapping more outgoing IR.

CO₂ has gone from 280 ppm (pre-industrial) to ~425 ppm. The physics of why this matters has been understood since Tyndall (1861) and Arrhenius (1896).
:::

---

## Try It: Mars's Equilibrium Temperature {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

**Mars:** $d = 1.52$ AU, $A = 0.25$

$$T_{\text{eq}} = 279\ \text{K} \times (1-0.25)^{1/4} \times \left(\frac{1.52}{1}\right)^{-1/2}$$

::: {.fragment}
$(0.75)^{1/4} \approx 0.930 \qquad (1.52)^{-1/2} \approx 0.811$

$$T_{\text{eq}} \approx 279 \times 0.930 \times 0.811 \approx 210\ \text{K}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.bg-muted .p-2 .text-sm}
Mars's actual surface temperature is **~210 K**. $T_{\text{eq}} \approx T_{\text{surface}}$ — the greenhouse effect is negligible. Why? CO$_2$ dominates (95%), but the atmosphere is only **0.6% of Earth's pressure**. Too thin to trap significant IR.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
51–52 min. Walk through the ratio method. Students should be comfortable with this from Lecture 2. The punchline: same greenhouse gas (CO₂) as Venus, but thin atmosphere → no warming. Atmospheric pressure matters as much as composition.
:::

---

## Quick Check: Greenhouse Physics {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {.quiz}
The greenhouse effect warms Earth because…

- [ ] CO$_2$ absorbs incoming visible sunlight
- [ ] The ozone layer traps heat
- [x] Atmospheric gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit some downward
- [ ] Earth's core heats the surface
:::

::: {.notes}
~53 min. Give 20 seconds.

Correct: greenhouse gases absorb outgoing IR (not incoming visible), re-emit in all directions including downward. This is Kirchhoff's law 3.
:::

---

## Two More Confusions to Clear Up

::: {.incremental}
- **"Stronger lines = more of that element."** Not necessarily. Line strength depends primarily on **temperature** — which levels are populated — not abundance. An A star doesn't have *more* hydrogen than an M star; it just has the right $T$ to populate $n = 2$.
- **"Absorption lines make a star dimmer."** Negligibly. Absorbed photons are re-emitted in random directions (resonant scattering). Total luminosity is conserved; the spectrum just has narrow dark features carved into it.
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-sm .text-muted .mt-2}
(Recall: we killed Myths 1 and 2 — spectral type ≠ composition, and redshift ≠ red star — at the start.)
:::

::: {.notes}
54–55 min. Two confusions, not four — the other two were moved to "Two Myths to Kill Now" early in the lecture. Students have already internalized those; these two are the subtler traps.
:::

---

## What Spectra Can't Tell Us (Directly)

::: {.incremental}
- **Mass** — need binary orbits + Doppler (Lecture 4)
- **Distance** — need parallax or other distance indicator (Lecture 1)
- **Age** — need stellar evolution models (Module 3)
- **Tangential velocity** — Doppler gives only the radial component
:::

::: {.fragment .text-center .text-base .text-muted .mt-2}
Spectra are powerful — but not omnipotent. Every tool has limits.
:::

::: {.notes}
55–56 min. Quick limitations slide. Keeps students honest about what one observation can and can't do. Sets up why we need binary stars (Lecture 4) and the H–R diagram (Lectures 5–6).
:::

---

## Summary: Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
1. **Kirchhoff's laws** connect spectral appearance to physical conditions — stars show absorption spectra because of their temperature gradient
2. **Spectral lines** are atomic fingerprints — energy levels set wavelengths
3. **OBAFGKM** is a **temperature** sequence — same composition, different excitation
4. **Doppler shift** converts wavelength shifts to velocities — $\Delta\lambda/\lambda_0 = v_r/c$
5. **Greenhouse effect** is Kirchhoff's law 3 applied to planets — same physics, different scale
:::

::: {.notes}
56–57 min. Read through once. Each takeaway maps to a learning objective.
:::

---

## The Takeaway {.center}

If you forget everything else from today, remember this:

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.r-fit-text}
**One spectrum → composition, temperature, velocity.**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .mt-2}
A star's light is an autobiography — if you know how to read it.
:::

::: {.notes}
~57 min. Let this land. This is the core message of the entire lecture.
